Let $\Sigma$ be a finite token alphabet, let $\mathtt{eos}\notin\Sigma$ be an end-of-sequence symbol, and let $d,L,H\ge1$ be fixed integers. For each length $n\ge1$, an input is $(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},\mathtt{eos})$. A symbol embedding assigns a vector $v_a\in\mathbb R^d$ to each $a\in\Sigma\cup\{\mathtt{eos}\}$; a positional embedding sequence assigns $p_i\in\mathbb R^d$ independent of the input symbols. A fixed shared input map gives $y_i^{(0)}=f_{\rm in}(v_{x_i},p_i)$. For each layer $k=1,\ldots,L$ and head $h=1,\ldots,H$, a fixed score map $s_{k,h}:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ gives scores $a_{i,j}^{(k,h)}=s_{k,h}(y_i^{(k-1)},y_j^{(k-1)})$ for every query position $i$ and key position $j$. In the soft model, $\widehat a_{i,\cdot}^{(k,h)}=\operatorname{softmax}(a_{i,\cdot}^{(k,h)})$. In the hard model, $\widehat a_{i,j}^{(k,h)}=1$ at the smallest index $j$ attaining $\max_{r\le n}a_{i,r}^{(k,h)}$ and is $0$ at other indices. With fixed value maps $V_{k,h}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and fixed positionwise maps $F_k:(\mathbb R^d)^{H+1}\to\mathbb R^d$, the update is

$$
b_{i,k,h}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\widehat a_{i,j}^{(k,h)}V_{k,h}(y_j^{(k-1)}),\qquad y_i^{(k)}=F_k(y_i^{(k-1)},b_{i,k,1},\ldots,b_{i,k,H}).
$$

Each score, value, and positionwise map is shared across positions and is fixed independently of $n$. In the hard-attention limit theorem, the score, value, and positionwise maps may be arbitrary fixed maps; no activation-function or parameter-norm bound is imposed. For the soft-influence theorem below, each score is a scaled dot product of fixed linear query and key projections, each value map is a fixed linear map, the token and positional embeddings are uniformly bounded over all positions and lengths, the combined initial states satisfy $\sup_{i\ge1,\ a\in\Sigma\cup\{\mathtt{eos}\}}\|f_{\rm in}(v_a,p_i)\|_2<\infty$, and every positionwise map is globally Lipschitz. The initial-state bound holds for addition or concatenation of bounded embeddings, but must be imposed separately for an arbitrary input map. A hard-attention recognizer classifies the input from $y_n^{(L)}$ after reading $\mathtt{eos}$. A soft next-token predictor applies a fixed linear logit map and softmax to $y_n^{(L)}$ to obtain a probability vector on a fixed finite alphabet.

derivations.claim: Choose $0<\eta<1/4$ so that $(1-2\eta)C>C'$, then choose $0<\delta<1$ and $0<q<1/(1+\delta)$ so that $(1-(1+\delta)q)(1-2\eta)C>C'$. Put $D=\lceil c/(\eta C)\rceil$ and regard $k\ge1$ as an integer parameter whose finitely many lower bounds will be fixed after the local-lemma estimates. For each position $j$, choose a support $S_j$ of at most $c$ currently free input positions determining its layer-zero activation. There are at most $cn$ incidences between supports and positions. Fix every free input position occurring in more than $D$ supports, using any fixed symbol. At most $cn/D\le\eta Cn$ positions are fixed; afterwards every free input position belongs to at most $D$ supports.

For a current restriction and query triple $(i,h,z)$, where $h$ is a head at position $i$ and $z$ is a possible layer-zero activation at $i$, at most $cD$ key positions have supports intersecting $S_i$; call these exceptional. For every other key position $j$, its support is disjoint from $S_i$, so the maximum score $m_j$ for query value $z$ is attainable by assigning its free support. Order these eligible positions by decreasing $m_j$, breaking ties by position, and put $R=\lceil cD(k+1)\rceil$. For all sufficiently large $n$, at least $R$ eligible positions exist. Greedily select $k$ among the first $R$ with pairwise disjoint supports: each choice removes at most $cD$ candidates because its support has at most $c$ symbols and each symbol occurs in at most $D$ supports. Record for each selected position a support assignment attaining its maximum.

If a selected support is fixed to its recorded maximum-attaining assignment, that key's score is at least $m_R$. Every eligible position after the first $R$ has maximum score at most $m_R$; equality is resolved in favor of a position among the first $R$ by the chosen tie order. Hence a head's winner lies among the exceptional positions or the first $R$ eligible positions. The first-layer output at position $i$ is therefore determined by $S_i$ and the supports of at most $Hs^c(cD+R)$ candidate key positions, one set for each possible query activation, head, and key. It depends on at most $c'=c+Hs^c c(cD+R)$ original input positions.

Starting from the restriction in step 1.1, repeatedly recompute the candidate sets in step 2.1 for every still-uncaptured triple. When a triple is captured, retain its current exceptional set and first-$R$ eligible positions as its candidate set. Its assigned cutoff key remains at least as highly scored as every later position in the old eligible ordering, since refinements leave its score fixed and can only decrease other attainable maxima; any position that later leaves the eligible set was already in the retained exceptional set. If some key activation is selected in more than $s^c kH$ uncaptured triples, one of its at most $s^c$ possible values is a recorded maximum for more than $kH$ of them. Fix its at most $c$ free input symbols to a support assignment producing that value. The query values of those triples remain unchanged, so all become captured. There are at most $s^cHn$ triples, so this process has at most $s^c n/k$ refinements and fixes at most $s^c c n/k$ additional symbols. Require $k$ large enough that $s^c c/k\le\eta C$. At termination at least $(1-2\eta)Cn$ inputs remain free, and each key activation is selected in at most $T=s^c kH$ uncaptured triples.

For each uncaptured triple $t=(i,h,z)$, let $X_t$ be the event that none of its $k$ selected supports is fixed to its recorded maximum-attaining assignment by the random restriction [A1]. An assignment on $r\le c$ free symbols has probability $(q/s)^r\ge(q/s)^c$. The selected supports are pairwise disjoint, so these assignment events are independent and $\mathbb P(X_t)\le a^k$, where $a=1-(q/s)^c<1$.

Let $m$ be the number of free inputs after step 3.2 and let $X_0$ be the event that more than $(1+\delta)qm$ of them are fixed by [A1]. For $Z\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,q)$ and $\mu=mq$, exponential Markov at $t=\log(1+\delta)$ gives $\mathbb P(Z\ge(1+\delta)\mu)\le e^{-t(1+\delta)\mu}(1-q+qe^t)^m\le e^{-\mu((1+\delta)\log(1+\delta)-\delta)}\le e^{-\delta^2\mu/3}$. The middle inequality uses $1+u\le e^u$. For the last, $g(\delta)=(1+\delta)\log(1+\delta)-\delta-\delta^2/3$ has $g(0)=0$ and $g'(\delta)=\log(1+\delta)-2\delta/3\ge0$ on $[0,1]$, since $\log(1+\delta)\ge2\delta/(2+\delta)\ge2\delta/3$. Consequently $\mathbb P(X_0)\le e^{-\alpha n}$, where $\alpha=\delta^2q(1-2\eta)C/3>0$.

For each event $X_t$, take its defining-coordinate set to be the union of its query support and its $k$ selected key supports. Join two $X_t$ events when these sets overlap, and join $X_0$ to every $X_t$. Each coordinate occurs in at most $DHs^c$ query supports: at most $D$ position supports contain it, and each such position has at most $Hs^c$ head-and-query-value triples. It occurs in at most $Ds^cT$ selected key supports: each of at most $D$ position supports has at most $s^c$ possible key activations, and each activation is selected in at most $T$ triples by step 3.2. Each event uses at most $c(k+1)$ coordinates, so its degree is at most $f=1+c(k+1)D(Hs^c+s^cT)=O(k^2)$. Non-neighbours' defining-coordinate sets are disjoint from the event's set; product independence therefore gives independence from every conjunction of their complements, as required by [F2]. Set $x_{X_0}=1/2$ and $x_{X_t}=1/k^2$. Since $a=1-(q/s)^c<1$ and $f=O(k^2)$, the quantity $k^{-2}(1/2)(1-k^{-2})^f$ is bounded below by a positive constant times $k^{-2}$ for large $k$, whereas $a^k$ decays exponentially. Thus the local-lemma condition holds for every $X_t$ once $k$ is sufficiently large.

There are at most $s^cHn$ events other than $X_0$. Its local-lemma condition follows if $e^{-\alpha n}\le\tfrac12(1-k^{-2})^{s^cHn}$. Choose $k$ large enough that $s^cH[-\log(1-k^{-2})]<\alpha$; the inequality then holds for all sufficiently large $n$. The stage-two, local-event, and $X_0$ requirements are finitely many eventual lower bounds on $k$, so they hold simultaneously for sufficiently large $k$. By [F2], a refinement avoiding $X_0$ and every $X_t$ exists.

Avoiding $X_0$ leaves at least $(1-(1+\delta)q)m\ge(1-(1+\delta)q)(1-2\eta)Cn>C'n$ free inputs by the choices in step 1.1. Avoiding every $X_t$ captures each remaining triple. For a captured triple, its retained cutoff key and candidate set from step 3.2 continue to block every later eligible position; for an uncaptured triple, step 6.1 fixes a cutoff key from its final candidate set. Step 3.1 therefore confines each head's winner to at most $cD+R$ candidate positions for each query value. Taking the union over at most $s^c$ query values and $H$ heads, together with the query support, gives the dependence bound $c'=c+Hs^c c(cD+R)$. Replacing each layer-zero activation by its first-layer output absorbs one layer while preserving the model's restricted computation.

Apply the one-layer reduction successively to the fixed $L$ layers, choosing intermediate fractions $C=C_0>C_1>\cdots>C_L=C'$. Each stage has a finite dependence bound and a finite length threshold. Since $L$ is finite, their maximum threshold is finite; beyond it, the final restriction leaves at least $C'n$ inputs free and the final output depends on a bounded number of original inputs. This proves the Statement.

Initially each free layer-zero state depends on its own input symbol. For all sufficiently large $n$, at least $0.99N$ positions are free, since only the end-marker position is fixed. Apply [F1] successively through the $L$ layers, using free fractions $0.99=C_0>C_1>\cdots>C_L=0.9$. For every sufficiently large $n$, this gives a restriction leaving at least $0.9N$ free word positions and a constant $c_L$ such that the classification output depends on at most $c_L$ input positions.

Now suppose the model recognizes $\mathrm{2DYCK}$. Its restriction to the two-symbol subalphabet consisting of one opening bracket and its matching closing bracket would recognize the one-type Dyck language, whose words have equal numbers of opening and closing brackets and nonnegative opening-minus-closing count at every prefix. Fix an even word length $n$, put $N=n+1$, and let $m=\lfloor n/5\rfloor$. Initially fix the first $m$ word symbols to the opening bracket and the last $m$ word symbols to the closing bracket; leave the middle symbols free and keep the end marker fixed. For all sufficiently large even $n$, at least $0.59N$ positions are free. By [F1], with final free fraction $0.55$, refine this restriction so the model output depends on at most $c_L$ input positions and at least $0.55N$ word positions remain free. If $t$ middle positions were additionally fixed, then $$ t\le n-2m-0.55N\le0.06N $$ for all sufficiently large $N$. Also $m\ge N/5-6/5$, so $m>t$.

Choose $n$ large enough that $0.9N>c_L$. Some free bit position $i$ is not among the at most $c_L$ positions determining the output. Complete the restriction arbitrarily to a word $w$, and let $w'$ be obtained by flipping bit $i$. Their model outputs agree because all input positions on which the output depends agree, but exactly one of $w,w'$ has an even number of ones. Thus no such model classifies all length-$n$ words exactly as $\mathrm{PARITY}$.

citations.quote: Let $\mathrm{PARITY}=\{w\in\{0,1\}^*: w\text{ contains an even number of }1\text{s}\}$. Let $\mathrm{2DYCK}$ be the language over $\{(,),[,]\}$ of words whose brackets are correctly balanced and properly nested by type. No fixed finite-depth hard-attention sequence model with a fixed finite number of heads, fixed maps independent of input length, and a fixed classification readout from its end-marker state classifies every sufficiently long input exactly as a member or nonmember of $\mathrm{PARITY}$; no such model recognizes $\mathrm{2DYCK}$ either. Exact recognition means that the model's binary output equals the language membership indicator for every input word, with the end marker appended before the model is evaluated.

Fix $p\in(0,1)$. Generate a bit string by a two-state process whose state is the parity of the number of emitted $1$s: in the even state it terminates with probability $p$, and otherwise emits $0$ or $1$ with probability $(1-p)/2$ each; in the odd state it emits $0$ or $1$ with probability $1/2$ each and cannot terminate. For each $n\ge2$, let $D_n$ be the law of length-$(n-1)$ prefixes conditional on the process emitting at least $n-1$ bits, and ask a fixed soft-attention model to predict the next symbol in $\{\mathtt{eos},0,1\}$ from that prefix followed by the end marker. Let $r_x$ be the true next-symbol distribution and let $q_n(x)$ be the model's predicted distribution. Define cross-entropy by $\operatorname{CE}(r,q)=-\sum_a r(a)\log q(a)$, with value $+\infty$ if $r(a)>0=q(a)$, and entropy by $H(r)=-\sum_{a:r(a)>0}r(a)\log r(a)$. Then every fixed soft-attention model satisfying the one-symbol influence hypotheses has

$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}\operatorname{CE}(r_x,q_n(x))\ge H(u),\qquad u(\mathtt{eos})=p/2,\quad u(0)=u(1)=(2-p)/4.$$
A constant predictor $q_n(x)=u$ attains $H(u)$ for every $n$, so $H(u)$ is the sharp unigram chance level. An arbitrary fixed predictor may have greater cross-entropy; this result gives no soft-attention exact-classification impossibility theorem.

Fix $p\in(0,1)$ and let $D_n$ be a probability law on valid length-$(n-1)$ prefixes over $\{(,),[, ]\}$. Let $E_n$ be a union of disjoint equal-mass pairs $\{x,x'\}$ in the support of $D_n$ such that each prefix in a pair ends in a closing bracket and has positive stack height after that bracket; $x'$ is obtained by changing the type of the top unmatched opening bracket in $x$, at a position before the final prefix symbol. Assume that, conditional on $x$, the next-symbol law assigns probability $p/2$ to each opening bracket and probability $1-p$ to the closing bracket matching its top unmatched opening, and that the law conditional on $x'$ swaps the two possible closing-bracket types while leaving the opening probabilities unchanged. If $D_n(E_n)\ge P_0>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$, then every fixed soft-attention predictor satisfying the one-symbol influence hypotheses has

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\bigl(\mathcal L_n-\mathcal L_n^*\bigr)\ge P_0(1-p)\log 2,
$$

where $\mathcal L_n$ is expected next-symbol cross-entropy and $\mathcal L_n^*=\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}H(r_x)$ is the optimal conditional cross-entropy. This lemma requires the positive-mass paired-prefix hypothesis; it does not assert that a particular PCFG supplies that hypothesis.

Fix $p\in(0,1)$. Independently expand each nonterminal of the grammar $S\to(S)S$, $S\to[S]S$, $S\to\epsilon$ with respective probabilities $p/2,p/2,1-p$, and read the yield from left to right. Equivalently, start with an empty bracket stack and repeatedly choose an opening bracket of either type with probability $p/2$ each, pushing its type; with probability $1-p$, close the top bracket when the stack is nonempty, or emit $\mathtt{eos}$ and stop when it is empty. This defines a probability law on finite words followed by $\mathtt{eos}$ and on infinite bracket streams. For a valid bracket prefix $x$, let $o(x),c(x)$ and $h(x)=o(x)-c(x)$ denote its opening count, closing count and final stack height. Its cylinder probability is
$$
w_p(x)=(p/2)^{o(x)}(1-p)^{c(x)}.
$$
For every $k\ge0$, let $s_{p,k}=\sum_{|x|=k}w_p(x)$, summing over valid prefixes, and define $D_{p,k}(x)=w_p(x)/s_{p,k}$. Thus $D_{p,k}$ conditions only on having emitted at least $k$ bracket tokens, without conditioning on eventual termination or exact total length. The target after a sampled prefix is its ordinary next token in the same process. At positive height its law assigns $p/2$ to each opening type and $1-p$ to the matching closing type.

For $k\ge3$, let $E_k$ consist of prefixes whose last three symbols are an opening of type $a$, an opening of type $b$, and the closing of type $b$, with $a,b$ independently ranging over the two types. These prefixes have positive final height and end in a closing bracket. Flipping the opening type $a$ at position $k-2$ is a fixed-point-free involution of $E_k$ into equal-mass pairs; paired prefixes differ only at this nonfinal position and their top unmatched opening types are opposite. Moreover,
$$
D_{p,k}(E_k)=p^2(1-p)\frac{s_{p,k-3}}{s_{p,k}}\ge p^2(1-p)>0.
$$

The finite-word mass of a typed Dyck word of length $2m$ is $(p/2)^m(1-p)^{m+1}$. The total finite-word mass is $q_p=1$ for $p\le1/2$ and $q_p=(1-p)/p$ for $p>1/2$. After conditioning on eventual termination, the finite-word probability law and all its prefix laws are exactly those of the preceding process with parameter $a=pq_p=\min(p,1-p)$; consequently its survival-conditioned prefixes have the same pairing bound $a^2(1-a)$. Conditioning instead on exact word length $2m$ yields the uniform law on typed Dyck words of that length, independently of $p$; that conditioning is different and does not retain the displayed next-token probabilities.

Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be a sequence matrix whose rows are token representations, and let $P$ be any $n\times n$ permutation matrix. Every finite composition $T$ of position-shared encoder layers built from unmasked multi-head self-attention, residual additions, rowwise layer normalization, and a shared positionwise feedforward map, with no positional encoding, satisfies

$$
T(PX)=P\,T(X).
$$

For a fixed attention mask $M$, the corresponding layer satisfies $\operatorname{Layer}_{PMP^{\mathsf T}}(PX)=P\operatorname{Layer}_{M}(X)$. Hence every permutation that leaves a fixed mask $M$ unchanged is an equivariance of the corresponding layer. The standard causal mask $M_{ij}=0$ for $j\le i$ and $M_{ij}=-\infty$ for $j>i$ is preserved only by the identity permutation.

For a sequence of length $n$ with $d$-dimensional token representations, a positional encoding is a fixed or trainable matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ added rowwise to the token matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, giving $X+P$. One fixed choice, with positions $s\in\mathbb N_0$ and coordinates indexed from $0$, is $P_{s,2r}=\sin(s/10000^{2r/d})$ and $P_{s,2r+1}=\cos(s/10000^{2r/d})$ whenever the indicated coordinate is less than $d$.

For decoder self-attention on $n$ positions indexed by $0,\ldots,n-1$, the causal mask is $M\in(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\})^{n\times n}$ with $M_{ij}=0$ when $j\le i$ and $M_{ij}=-\infty$ when $j>i$. Thus query position $i$ can use keys at positions $0,\ldots,i$ and cannot use a future position; every row has an allowed key because $M_{ii}=0$.

For a grid column $x=(a_1\delta,\ldots,a_d\delta)$, where $a_i\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$, its scalar code is $$\ell(x)=u^{\mathsf T}x,\qquad \ell(x)/\delta=a_1+a_2m+\cdots+a_dm^{d-1}.$$ Thus the valid column codes are distinct multiples of $\delta$ in $[0,B]$, where $B=\delta(q-1)$. If a column has a sentinel coordinate $-\delta^{-nd}$, the sum of all its other coordinate contributions is at most $\delta^{-d+1}-1$, so its code is at most $-\delta^{-nd}+\delta^{-d+1}-1<0$.

For a scalar threshold $b$, the single-head update $$ \psi(Z;b)=e_1(u^{\mathsf T}Z)\operatorname{hmax}\!\left((u^{\mathsf T}Z)^{\mathsf T}(u^{\mathsf T}Z-b\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T})\right) $$ is an allowed attention update contribution: its key and value projections are $u$, its query projection is $u$ with bias $-b$, and its output vector is $e_1$. In query column $j$, if $\ell_j>b$ it returns the largest current scalar code, and if $\ell_j<b$ it returns the smallest. If $\ell_j=b$, all query scores are zero and equal-weight hardmax returns the mean $\bar\ell=n^{-1}\sum_k\ell_k$. Thus, writing $\ell_{\max}=\max_k\ell_k$ and $\ell_{\min}=\min_k\ell_k$, the contribution $\psi(Z;b)-\psi(Z;b')$ for $b<b'$ is $\ell_{\max}-\ell_{\min}$ in the first coordinate when $b<\ell_j<b'$, $\bar\ell-\ell_{\min}$ when $\ell_j=b$, $\ell_{\max}-\bar\ell$ when $\ell_j=b'$, and zero when $\ell_j<b$ or $\ell_j>b'$. In particular, if no current code equals either threshold, it shifts exactly the columns strictly between them by $\ell_{\max}-\ell_{\min}$.

Sweep the valid scalar codes $0,\delta,\ldots,B$ in increasing order, using the two-head update $\;Z\mapsto Z+q(\psi(Z;\ell-\delta/2)-\psi(Z;\ell+\delta/2))\;$ at code $\ell$. All initial codes, including sentinel codes, are multiples of $\delta$: every grid coordinate lies in $\delta\mathbb Z$ and every entry of $u$ is an integer. Since $q=m^d$ is an integer, each strict selective shift preserves this lattice; inductively no current code can equal any half-grid threshold $\ell\pm\delta/2$. This also applies to duplicate-column inputs and to the position-tagged lattice. For $L\in\widehat G_\delta$, order its distinct column codes as $\ell_1<\cdots<\ell_n$. The first sweep shifts only $\ell_1$ to $\widetilde\ell_1=\ell_1+q(\ell_n-\ell_1)>B$, since $\ell_n-\ell_1\ge\delta$ and $q\delta=B+\delta$. Each later sweep shifts the next unmodified code and gives $$ \widetilde\ell_j=\ell_j+q(\widetilde\ell_{j-1}-\ell_j)>\widetilde\ell_{j-1}\qquad(2\le j\le n). $$ Thus shifted columns leave all later threshold intervals, and the final scalar codes satisfy $0<\widetilde\ell_1<\cdots<\widetilde\ell_n$.

Write $g_j=\ell_{j+1}-\ell_j\ge\delta$. Unrolling the recurrence in step 2.1 gives $$ t:=\widetilde\ell_n=\ell_n+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(q^n-q^{n-j})g_j. $$ Consequently $$\delta q^{n-1}(q-1)\le t\le \delta q^n(q-1)-\delta(q-1)^2.$$ The lower bound follows from the $j=1$ term; the upper bound follows from $\ell_n\le B$ and $\sum_jg_j\le B$. The map $(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n)\mapsto t$ is injective: if two ordered tuples give the same $t$, put $a_j=(\ell_j-\ell'_j)/\delta\in\mathbb Z$, so $|a_j|\le q-1$. The difference equation is $$ a_n+q(a_{n-1}-a_n)+\cdots+q^{n-1}(a_1-a_2)+q^n(a_n-a_1)=0. $$ Reduction modulo $q$ first gives $a_n=0$; division by $q$ and repeated reduction modulo $q$ then gives $a_{n-1}=0,\ldots,a_1=0$. Hence distinct unordered column multisets have distinct $t$ values, separated by at least $\delta$.

Apply one final single-head update $Z\mapsto Z+K\psi(Z;0)$, with a positive integer $K$. For valid $L$, all $\widetilde\ell_j>0$, so it adds $Kt$ to every first coordinate and changes the scalar codes to $$ c_{L,j}=Kt+\widetilde\ell_j. $$ For different column multisets, their $t$ values differ by at least $\delta$, while $0<\widetilde\ell_j\le t$. Choose $K$ so that $K\delta>\max t$ over the finite valid grid. The intervals $[Kt,Kt+t]$ for different multisets are disjoint, and codes within one multiset are distinct by step 2.1. All resulting codes are multiples of $\delta$, hence distinct codes are at least $\delta$ apart.

If $L$ has duplicate columns but no sentinel, its scalar codes have only $r<n$ distinct levels. The same sweep shifts these $r$ levels, and its largest value is at most $\delta q^r(q-1)-\delta(q-1)^2\le\delta q^{n-1}(q-1)-\delta(q-1)^2$, strictly below the lower bound for valid $t$ in step 3.1. A sentinel column has a negative code by step 1.1 and remains the minimum throughout the sweep. If all codes are negative, the final update in step 4.1 shifts every code further negative. If some codes are nonnegative, the first nonnegative code is shifted by at least $q(q^n-B)>\delta q^{n+1}$; the later positive codes are shifted by still larger amounts. This exceeds every valid $t$ in step 3.1. Thus, after the final update, each invalid scalar code has one of three forms: below every valid code, above every valid code, or negative. Since there are finitely many grid inputs and all codes are multiples of $\delta$, choose $K$ large enough that every invalid code lies at least $\delta$ outside the interval from the least to the greatest valid code.

The preceding construction gives a finite scalar code for each token of each valid context; these codes are all distinct, and column permutations carry each code and its token to the corresponding permuted token by [F2]. Let $\lambda_-$ and $\lambda_+$ be the least and greatest valid codes. Because the table $A$ and grid are finite, enlarge $K$ so that $|u^{\mathsf T}A(L)_{:,j}|<\lambda_- -\delta/3$ for every valid $L,j$. A three-piece constant activation that is zero on $[\lambda_- -\delta/3,\lambda_+ +\delta/3]$ and one outside this interval detects exactly the invalid codes. Subtracting a constant larger than the maximum absolute coordinate of every encoded grid state makes every invalid state strictly negative; for each coordinate $r$, the allowed residual update $Z\mapsto Z+e_r\operatorname{ReLU}(-e_r^{\mathsf T}Z)$ replaces that coordinate by $z_r+\max(0,-z_r)=\max(0,z_r)$. These $d$ updates send every invalid state to zero and leave every valid, coordinatewise nonnegative state unchanged. For each valid code $c_{L,j}$, a three-piece pulse equal to one on $[-\delta/3,\delta/3]$ and zero outside, applied to $u^{\mathsf T}Z-c_{L,j}$, selects exactly its token. Add the vector $A(L)_{:,j}-Z_{:,j}$ at that token. The updated token has scalar value $u^{\mathsf T}A(L)_{:,j}$ below every code, so later pulses cannot select it; the remaining tokens retain their codes until selected. Equivariance of $A$ makes each update correct for every permutation of $L$. This yields $A(L)$ on $\widehat G_\delta$ and zero on every other point of $G_\delta^+$.

For the position-tagged grid, the scalar code of column $j$ has the form $$ \ell_j=(j-1)S+r_j,\qquad S=\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\delta^{-k},\quad 0\le r_j\le B,\quad r_j\in\delta\mathbb Z. $$ Since $S-B\ge\delta$, codes in a matrix satisfy $\ell_1<\cdots<\ell_n$ and each individual code identifies its column vector. Choose an integer $Q\ge q$ with $Q\delta>(n-1)S+B$. Sweep all possible position-tagged scalar codes in increasing order, replacing the shift multiplier $q$ in step 2.1 by $Q$. All codes remain in $\delta\mathbb Z$, so none equals a half-grid threshold. Since distinct initial codes differ by at least $\delta$, the first shifted code exceeds the largest possible initial code, and each subsequent shifted code exceeds its predecessor. Thus the recurrence of step 2.1 holds with $Q$ in place of $q$, and different matrices give different ordered tuples $(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n)$. The divisibility argument in step 3.1 applies modulo $Q$: for each fixed position, the offsets $(j-1)S$ cancel and the difference of two $r_j$ values divided by $\delta$ has magnitude at most $q-1<Q$. **Inputs:** A nonempty source token sequence $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, a target prefix $(y_0,\ldots,y_{m-1})$ with $m\ge1$ and a start token $y_0$, source and target embedding maps into $\mathbb R^d$, positional encoding matrices of compatible shapes, a finite encoder stack, a finite decoder stack, and a linear output map to a finite vocabulary of logits. Each layer has the parameters and conventions in the transformer encoder/decoder definition. All self-attention and cross-attention masks must leave at least one allowed key in every query row.

**Procedure:**

1. Embed each source token and add its positional vector to form $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$.
2. Apply the encoder layers in order to $X$ and call the final matrix $E\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$.
3. Embed each target-prefix token and add its positional vector to form $U\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$.
4. Apply each decoder layer in order. In every decoder layer, use the causal mask on decoder self-attention, use the current decoder rows as queries and $E$ as keys and values for cross-attention, and then apply the positionwise feedforward sublayer.
5. Apply the output linear map to each final decoder row and apply softmax over vocabulary coordinates. Return the encoder matrix $E$, the final decoder hidden matrix, and the rowwise next-token probability matrix.

**Outputs:** The source representations, decoder representations, and one probability vector for each target-prefix position. At position $i$, the decoder self-attention calculation uses only target-prefix positions $j\le i$; the encoder cross-attention may use every source position.

For finite real scores, every softmax weight is strictly positive, so each output row uses the value row of every input position. This is one direct attention edge; composing $L$ layers yields at most one such edge per layer, hence at most $L$ attention edges independent of $n$.
Summing over $h$ heads with total width $\sum_{a=1}^h d_h^{(a)}=d$ gives $O(n^2d)$ score and value work. Normalizing $n$ rows of $n$ scores costs $O(n^2)$, which is at most $O(n^2d)$ because $d\ge1$.

Let $n_q,n_k,d_k,d_v$ be positive integers, let $Q\in\mathbb R^{n_q\times d_k}$ and $K\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times d_k}$ be query and key matrices, and let $V\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times d_v}$ be a value matrix. For a real matrix $S$ with $n_q$ rows and $n_k$ columns, define its row softmax by $\operatorname{softmax}_{\rm row}(S)_{ij}=\exp(S_{ij})/\sum_{\ell=1}^{n_k}\exp(S_{i\ell})$. The scaled dot-product attention output is

$$
\operatorname{Attn}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}_{\rm row}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\mathsf T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\in\mathbb R^{n_q\times d_v}.
$$

Each output row is the weighted average of the value rows, with weights given by the softmax of that query's scaled dot products with all keys. A mask is an array $M\in(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\})^{n_q\times n_k}$ whose entries are $0$ for allowed query-key pairs and $-\infty$ for disallowed pairs; masked attention replaces the score matrix by $QK^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{d_k}+M$ before row softmax and is defined only when every row has at least one allowed key. Here $\exp(-\infty)=0$.

For a sequence of length $n$ with $d$-dimensional token representations, a positional encoding is a fixed or trainable matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ added rowwise to the token matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, giving $X+P$. One fixed choice, with positions $s\in\mathbb N_0$ and coordinates indexed from $0$, is $P_{s,2r}=\sin(s/10000^{2r/d})$ and $P_{s,2r+1}=\cos(s/10000^{2r/d})$ whenever the indicated coordinate is less than $d$.

For decoder self-attention on $n$ positions indexed by $0,\ldots,n-1$, the causal mask is $M\in(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\})^{n\times n}$ with $M_{ij}=0$ when $j\le i$ and $M_{ij}=-\infty$ when $j>i$. Thus query position $i$ can use keys at positions $0,\ldots,i$ and cannot use a future position; every row has an allowed key because $M_{ii}=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, fix integers $d\ge1$ and $n\ge2$, and fix $1\le p<\infty$. For a matrix $Y\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}$, let $\|Y\|_p=(\sum_{r=1}^d\sum_{j=1}^n|Y_{rj}|^p)^{1/p}$, and for measurable maps on $\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ define
$$
d_p(f,g)=\left(\int_{\mathbb R^{dn}}\|f(X)-g(X)\|_p^p\,dX\right)^{1/p},
$$
using $dn$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Let $\mathcal T^{2,1,4}$ be the finite compositions of the two-head, head-size-one Yun blocks with tokenwise ReLU feedforward width four and no layer normalization. If $f:\mathbb R^{d\times n}\to\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ is continuous, has compact support, and satisfies $f(XP)=f(X)P$ for every $n\times n$ permutation matrix $P$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $g\in\mathcal T^{2,1,4}$ with $d_p(f,g)<\varepsilon$.

For every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ and every continuous $f:K\to\mathbb R^{d\times n}$, with no permutation condition, there are a trainable positional matrix $E\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ and $g\in\mathcal T^{2,1,4}$ such that
$$
\left(\int_K\|f(X)-g(X+E)\|_p^p\,dX\right)^{1/p}<\varepsilon.
$$

Let $\mathrm{PARITY}=\{w\in\{0,1\}^*: w\text{ contains an even number of }1\text{s}\}$. Let $\mathrm{2DYCK}$ be the language over $\{(,),[,]\}$ of words whose brackets are correctly balanced and properly nested by type. No fixed finite-depth hard-attention sequence model with a fixed finite number of heads, fixed maps independent of input length, and a fixed classification readout from its end-marker state classifies every sufficiently long input exactly as a member or nonmember of $\mathrm{PARITY}$; no such model recognizes $\mathrm{2DYCK}$ either. Exact recognition means that the model's binary output equals the language membership indicator for every input word, with the end marker appended before the model is evaluated.

Fix $p\in(0,1)$. Generate a bit string by a two-state process whose state is the parity of the number of emitted $1$s: in the even state it terminates with probability $p$, and otherwise emits $0$ or $1$ with probability $(1-p)/2$ each; in the odd state it emits $0$ or $1$ with probability $1/2$ each and cannot terminate. For each $n\ge2$, let $D_n$ be the law of length-$(n-1)$ prefixes conditional on the process emitting at least $n-1$ bits, and ask a fixed soft-attention model to predict the next symbol in $\{\mathtt{eos},0,1\}$ from that prefix followed by the end marker. Let $r_x$ be the true next-symbol distribution and let $q_n(x)$ be the model's predicted distribution. Define cross-entropy by $\operatorname{CE}(r,q)=-\sum_a r(a)\log q(a)$, with value $+\infty$ if $r(a)>0=q(a)$, and entropy by $H(r)=-\sum_{a:r(a)>0}r(a)\log r(a)$. Then every fixed soft-attention model satisfying the one-symbol influence hypotheses has

$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}\operatorname{CE}(r_x,q_n(x))\ge H(u),\qquad u(\mathtt{eos})=p/2,\quad u(0)=u(1)=(2-p)/4.$$
A constant predictor $q_n(x)=u$ attains $H(u)$ for every $n$, so $H(u)$ is the sharp unigram chance level. An arbitrary fixed predictor may have greater cross-entropy; this result gives no soft-attention exact-classification impossibility theorem.

derivations.claim: Under Countable Choice, apply [F1] separately for each integer $2\le n\le N$, each fixed $d\ge1$, each $1\le p<\infty$, and each chosen positive tolerance, to a target satisfying its corresponding continuity, compactness, and symmetry hypotheses. The theorem's existential network may depend on both $n$ and the tolerance; it gives no shared parameter set or depth bound uniform in $n$.

[F2] fixes one model across all lengths and asserts failure of exact recognition for sufficiently large PARITY and 2DYCK inputs. [F3] likewise fixes one soft model and gives a liminf lower bound for expected cross-entropy on a specified source. Neither statement contradicts the separate fixed-length approximation claims, whose metric is integrated $L_p$ error and whose parameters may vary with length.

derivations.claim: In a left-to-right grammar expansion, expanding the current $S$ nontrivially emits its opening bracket and leaves an inner $S$, its matching closing bracket, and a following $S$. Choosing $\epsilon$ finishes the current $S$ and either emits the pending matching close or, when no close is pending, ends the word. Thus each token is generated by precisely the stack transition stated above. The remaining choices after any finite emitted prefix are fresh independent choices. This constructs the stream law directly, including on nonterminating samples. Each valid prefix uniquely specifies the transition choices so far: every opening requires its type choice and every closing requires an epsilon choice. Their product is $w_p(x)$. In particular $s_{p,k}$ is the probability of reaching $k$ bracket tokens, is positive (all-open prefixes have positive probability), and is nonincreasing in $k$. Conditioning on reaching $k$ does not constrain the fresh choice after the prefix.

The grammar is unambiguous: a nonempty Dyck word has a unique first opening, its matching closing, and the resulting inside and following Dyck words, which recursively determine the derivation. A word with $m$ bracket pairs has $m$ nonempty choices and $m+1$ epsilon leaves, proving its stated finite-word mass. To calculate total termination mass, the probabilities of trees having height below successive finite bounds start at $q_0=0$ and satisfy $q_{j+1}=1-p+pq_j^2$. Their increasing limit is the probability of a finite tree: every finite binary tree has finite height, and an infinite finitely branching tree cannot have bounded height. The limit is the least fixed point in $[0,1]$, since iteration from zero stays below any nonnegative fixed point. The roots are $1$ and $(1-p)/p$, giving the stated $q_p$. The stream is finite exactly when the derivation is finite: every nonempty expansion emits an opening and any derivation with only finitely many nonempty expansions has only finitely many nodes.

Each prefix in $E_k$ is uniquely $u\,a\,b\,\overline b$, where $u$ is a valid prefix of length $k-3$. Such an extension is always valid, has height $h(u)+1$, and has the $a$-opening as its top unmatched opening. Its cylinder weight is $w_p(u)(p/2)^2(1-p)$. Summing the four choices of $a,b$ and then all $u$ gives $p^2(1-p)s_{p,k-3}$. Divide by $s_{p,k}$ and use monotonicity from step 1.1 to obtain the bound. Flipping $a$ changes no count, leaves the suffix pattern valid, and changes only position $k-2$; applying the flip twice restores the prefix. There are no fixed points, so its orbits are disjoint equal-mass pairs with swapped closing targets.

After a valid prefix of height $h$, the left-to-right residual derivation contains exactly $h+1$ still independent $S$ subtrees (and $h$ pending closing brackets). Its probability of eventual termination is therefore $q_p^{h+1}$. Consequently the termination-conditioned prefix cylinder is $w_p(x)q_p^{h(x)+1}/q_p=(pq_p/2)^{o(x)}((1-p)/q_p)^{c(x)}$. The fixed-point equation gives $(1-p)/q_p=1-pq_p$. This is exactly $w_a(x)$ with $a=pq_p$. The finite-word laws likewise agree, either by the same calculation including the final epsilon or directly from step 1.2. Applying step 2.1 with $a$ gives its pairing bound. Finally all typed Dyck words of a fixed length have the same mass by step 1.2 and there are finitely many of them, proving the uniform exact-length law and the asserted distinction of conditioning.
